about_page_description: DarcStar Technologies builds GIDE — a real-time control engine with safety properties formally verified against stated system and environment assumptions.
about_lead: DarcStar Technologies builds GIDE — the Guaranteed Intelligent Dynamics Engine: one real-time control system whose safety properties are formally verified against stated system and environment assumptions, specialized at compile time across robotics, financial markets, and software that improves itself.
about_mission_body_1: Autonomous systems are moving into places where failure is not an option — aircraft, industrial robots, live markets. Conventional testing can show that a controller usually behaves; it can never show that it will never violate a safety constraint.
about_mission_body_2: We close that gap by treating safety as something to prove rather than something to measure. GIDE's safety properties are stated as theorems and machine-checked in Lean 4 and Isabelle — over the mathematical model, under assumptions we name rather than leave implicit.
about_principle_proof_body: Safety properties are stated as theorems and machine-checked in Lean 4 and Isabelle — Control Barrier Functions verified against declared assumptions, not inferred from passing test runs.
about_principle_realtime_body: Closed-form continuous-time inference runs in microseconds, measured on hardware — fast enough to run the verified control law inside a live loop rather than offline. The timing is measured; no latency bound is proven.
about_principle_oneengine_body: GIDE specializes at compile time instead of re-implementing control per problem, so the same verified core runs from quadrotors to financial markets.
about_cta_body: If you are building autonomous systems where a safety guarantee has to hold, we would like to hear from you.
evidence_page_description: Every major claim on darcstar.tech, scoped: what was measured or proven, how, under which assumptions — and what remains outside the claim.
evidence_lead: Every number and safety claim on this site, stated precisely: what was measured or proven, how it was measured, under which assumptions — and where the boundary of the claim sits.
evidence_read_body: Each card states one claim exactly as the site makes it, with its date or release version, the environment and methodology behind it, and — just as deliberately — what it does not cover. When a figure is re-measured, the card is updated with it: these are dated claims, not slogans.
evidence_boundary_body: We keep two vocabularies apart. Proven means machine-checked in a proof assistant, over exact real arithmetic, about the mathematical model. Measured means benchmarked on hardware, with the sample counts and environment on record. Latency numbers are measured, never proven; safety theorems are proven, never inferred from test runs. The bridge between the real-number model and the floating-point implementation is checked numerically at runtime by an SMT solver portfolio — it is not itself a theorem.
evidence_cfc_claim: A single closed-form continuous-time (CfC) cell — the reference inference kernel — completes one forward pass in {latency} on average.
evidence_cfc_environment: x86_64 with AVX2; compiled with zig cc (Clang) at -O3 -march=native -ffast-math on the Zig 0.14.0-dev toolchain current at the time of measurement. The run predates our hardware-attribution harness, so the exact CPU model behind this figure is not on record — a gap we log rather than hide.
evidence_cfc_method: Arithmetic mean over 10,000 sequential inference calls after 1,000 warmup iterations, cross-checked on independently attributed hardware. Every run — environment, figures, attribution — is published on the benchmarks page.
evidence_cfc_not_covered: This is the reference kernel, not a deployed controller — deployed controllers are substantially larger and complete in the tens of microseconds, still inside the real-time budget. And no latency figure is formally proven: timing is measured, never a theorem.
evidence_cfc_artifacts: The benchmark harness, per-run logs, and a hardware-attribution ledger live in the GIDE repository; nightly CI re-runs the suite on attributed runners and publishes the results.
evidence_realtime_dated: Derived from the measured {latency} · 100 Hz control budget
evidence_realtime_claim: {multiple} is a derived margin, not a separate measurement: a 100 Hz control loop budgets 10 ms per tick, and 10 ms ÷ {latency} ≈ {multiple}.
evidence_realtime_method: The numerator is the control-loop period GIDE targets (100 Hz); the denominator is the measured mean kernel latency above. The margin therefore inherits every scope caveat of the 0.767 µs figure.
evidence_realtime_not_covered: The multiple applies to the reference kernel. Deployed controllers are larger and slower — see the hardware runs — yet still clear the same 10 ms budget by roughly two orders of magnitude. No real-time bound is formally proven.
evidence_theorems_claim: {checked} theorems in the GIDE framework are machine-checked. {complete} of those are complete — mechanized end-to-end in both Lean 4 and Isabelle/HOL with zero local axioms. The other {axiomBacked} are machine-checked modulo explicitly declared local axioms: named real-analysis backbones, each documented and tracked for discharge.
evidence_theorems_provers: Lean 4 v4.30.0 with Mathlib and Isabelle2025-2 with AFP 2026-06-01, both pinned by digest in container images. Runtime numerical checking uses an SMT portfolio: Z3 4.16.0, CVC5 1.3.4, Yices2 2.6.5, dReal 4.21.06.2.
evidence_theorems_method: Zero sorry placeholders across the corpus. Headline theorems must check in both provers independently; a negative-control suite of deliberately false variants must fail to compile; proof mutation testing and catalog-conformance gates run in CI on every change.
evidence_theorems_not_covered: The proofs are over exact real arithmetic: they cover the mathematical model, not the compiled floating-point implementation — that bridge is checked numerically at runtime, and closing it formally is open, tracked work. Framework assumptions (Lipschitz continuity, compact sets, bounded disturbance, hardware isolation) are declared inputs, not theorems.
evidence_theorems_artifacts: The theorem catalog and the runtime conformance registry are kept consistent by a CI census gate; tagged releases ship with a SHA-256 checksum manifest.
evidence_safety_dated: Complete, zero-axiom theorem cluster · Lean 4 + Isabelle/HOL
evidence_safety_claim: The safety core is a cluster of complete theorems — machine-checked end-to-end in both provers with zero local axioms — covering forward invariance of the safety set and Control Barrier Function filtering.
evidence_safety_proved: Nagumo forward invariance: a barrier that starts non-negative and satisfies the inward-rate condition stays non-negative for all forward time. Existence of a safe control under the CBF condition, and that the minimally-invasive CBF-QP leaves an already-feasible nominal control unmodified. Robustness of the invariance argument under learning updates, effective safety margin under measured latency, and keep-out-set feasibility including preservation under zero-order hold.
evidence_safety_assumptions: Controllability is carried as a named hypothesis, not re-proven. Safety margins are constant or linear-rate — general nonlinear class-K rates are out of scope. Dynamics are deterministic with bounded disturbance; the keep-out results are static state bounds, not general obstacle avoidance.
evidence_safety_not_covered: No microsecond or latency bound is proven anywhere in the proof corpus — any "proven microsecond safety" phrasing would be false, and we do not use it. Stochastic settings are out of scope. As above, the theorems govern the real-number model; the floating-point implementation is checked numerically at runtime.
evidence_domains_dated: One verified core, specialized at compile time
evidence_domains_claim: Every domain listed here builds and runs end-to-end against the same verified core. Shipped means the domain exists as a working subsystem with its own harness — maturity varies and is stated per domain below, not rounded up.
evidence_domain_cartpole_body: The original demonstration domain: 3D cart-pole balancing with machine-checked CBF safety filtering.
evidence_domain_quadrotor_body: 6-DOF rigid-body dynamics under a hybrid cascade controller, with the deployed configuration benchmarked end-to-end.
evidence_domain_markets_body: Live FX market data and paper trading against the Oanda API, driven by a 36-objective training curriculum.
evidence_domain_llm_body: Entropy, grounding, and safety regulation for language-model control behind a multi-tier governance pipeline.
evidence_domain_selfdev_body: The youngest domain: an autonomous spec → build → verify loop, currently approaching its first fully autonomous cycle — we say so rather than round up.
evidence_ip_heading: What we deliberately do not publish
evidence_ip_body: The cards above are designed to make our claims falsifiable without opening the engine. The following stay private: core source code, proof-generation automation, model weights, the controller architecture, optimization methods, customer data, and complete proof scripts.
evidence_ip_access_body: Under NDA we can provide an evaluation dossier, run a black-box benchmark on hardware you control, or arrange supervised inspection of sensitive artifacts in a controlled environment.
evidence_bench_page_description: Every benchmark figure behind darcstar.tech, run by run: methodology, environment, and attribution.
evidence_bench_lead: The run-level detail behind the latency figures: how each number was measured, on what, with the attribution behind it — including the gaps we log rather than hide.
evidence_bench_kernel_method: Arithmetic mean over 10,000 sequential inference calls after 1,000 warmup iterations, nanosecond-precision monotonic timing with compiler barriers.
evidence_bench_rerun_arm_body: A fully hardware-attributed run on a Neoverse-N2 (Clang 21.1.0) measures 0.75 µs mean with 0.76 µs p99 — within a few percent of the reference figure.
evidence_bench_rerun_x86_body: Committed x86 re-runs land between 0.81 and 0.91 µs mean.
evidence_bench_controller_body: A deployed end-to-end controller measures ≈52 µs p50 / ≈94 µs p99 — the figure to cite for whole-controller latency. It clears the 10 ms real-time budget by roughly 190×.
evidence_proofs_page_description: What machine-checked means at DarcStar: the definition of proven, the provers and checkers behind it, the verification methodology, and the trust boundary.
evidence_proofs_lead: The definition behind the theorem count: what qualifies as proven, which provers check it, how the proofs are stress-tested, and where the boundary of the guarantee sits.
evidence_proofs_definition_body: A theorem counts as machine-checked only when a proof assistant accepts it end-to-end. Complete theorems are mechanized independently in both Lean 4 and Isabelle/HOL with zero local axioms. Axiom-backed theorems are machine-checked modulo explicitly declared local axioms — named real-analysis backbones, each documented and tracked for discharge. Nothing in between is counted as proven.
evidence_proofs_axioms_body: Both words appear in the definition above, and a reader who meets them in one paragraph will reasonably take them for one thing. They are not, and the difference decides which of them is debt. They are also not a split of one number: local axioms are what separate complete theorems from axiom-backed ones, while the assumptions sit underneath both.
evidence_proofs_axioms_assumptions_title: Assumptions the theorems are stated under
evidence_proofs_axioms_assumptions_body: Lipschitz continuity, compact sets, bounded disturbance, hardware isolation and their siblings are hypotheses — declared once in a single registry and cited by the theorems that use them. They apply at every proof status, the complete theorems included: a complete proof is one that introduces no axiom of its own, not one that needs no assumptions. These are not debt. The work is to state them and keep them honest, not to remove them.
evidence_proofs_axioms_local_body: An axiom-backed proof declares, as a named axiom, a result it does not derive — general mathematics the prover libraries do not yet formalize: real-analysis and measure-theoretic backbones, textbook results rather than claims about our system. A proof may instead carry a result established elsewhere in the corpus that it does not yet build on. Either way it is debt: each is documented and tracked for discharge, and carrying even one is exactly what keeps a theorem out of the complete count.
evidence_proofs_axioms_carried_body: Where a proof mechanizes a theorem's mathematical shell but a physical fact the framework cannot prove — a hardware, floating-point or reconfiguration premise — is carried as an explicit named hypothesis, the implication is machine-checked and the theorem is still not counted as proven. Those results sit outside both figures published on this site.

privacy_page_description: How DarcStar Technologies collects, uses, and protects the personal information you share through this site.
privacy_lead: What we collect through this site, why we collect it, where it lives, and how to ask us about it — in plain language.
privacy_overview_body: DarcStar Technologies operates this website from the United States. We collect only the information you choose to share through the forms on this site, plus the minimal technical data needed to keep the site secure. We don't run advertising, we don't use third-party analytics or tracking cookies, and we never sell personal information. This policy covers darcstar.tech — if anything here is unclear, email us at the address at the bottom of this page.
privacy_collect_intro: Everything below is volunteered by you, except the security data noted last.
privacy_collect_contact_body: Your name, email address, message, and — if you choose to add them — your company and area of interest. We use these to read and respond to your message.
privacy_collect_waitlist_body: Your name and email address, plus optional details you can add: your organization, your country or region, and whether you would like occasional product and research updates (a preference we act on only by emailing you to confirm it — see “How we use it”). If you continue past the signup, the short optional questions also record your role, primary application and evaluation timeline — and, for commercial or operational use cases, how you address the problem today, a rough range for the annual value involved and for the budget you could consider for an initial evaluation, and what evidence you would need before adopting. The last step records either whether you would consider a paid evaluation, a short description of the deployment you have in mind, whether we may contact you directly, and how (including a phone number if you choose to give one) — or, if you are following the work rather than evaluating it, which kinds of update you would find useful. We use these to manage early access and to prioritize evaluations. The value and budget answers are for our internal prioritization only: we never show them back to you and we never publish them.
privacy_collect_account_body: Your name, email address, and a password when you create an account. The password is stored only as a salted hash — we can't read it. Sign-up is protected by Cloudflare Turnstile, which may process technical signals from your browser to tell humans from bots. Once you verify your email, contact messages sent from that same address — including ones sent before you signed up — are linked to your account so you can see them on your account page.
privacy_collect_technical_body: To protect the site we record the IP address and browser user-agent of sign-in attempts, and each contact or waitlist submission is stored with your browser's user-agent and a shortened hash of your IP address, which we use to rate-limit abuse. The only cookies the site sets are essential ones: the cookie that keeps you signed in, and — once you start the waitlist signup — a cookie that remembers which step of that form you reached, so reloading the page doesn't send you back to the beginning. It expires within a day, we never share it, and you can clear it at any time with the “Start a new signup” link on the form. There are no advertising or analytics cookies, and your language preference lives in the page address, not a cookie.
privacy_use_body: We use your information to respond to messages, run the early-access waitlist, operate your account, and keep the site secure. Email from us falls into two categories, and we treat them differently:
privacy_use_operational_body: Sent because you asked us for something: a reply to your message, your waitlist confirmation and any early-access invitation that follows it, and account mail like email verification and password resets. Joining the waitlist is a request for early access, so we write to you about it — that isn't a marketing list, and you can ask us to take you off it at any time. The note asking you to confirm optional updates is described below.
privacy_use_updates_body: Separate from early access, and entirely optional: the tick box on the waitlist form asks whether you would like occasional product and research updates, and the question at the end of that form records which kinds you would find useful — a content preference, not a permission. Because anyone can type someone else's address into a form like ours, a ticked box on its own is not permission to send. All it does is cause one email, asking you to confirm the address is yours; nothing else is sent unless you answer it, and we ask at most once a day however many times the form is filled in. That email — and every update, if and when we send any — carries a link that stops us without signing in: use it and we will not write to you about updates again, or ask again. We are still not sending product and research updates; what exists today is the consent step that has to come first. None of this touches your place on the early-access waitlist, or the operational email above.
privacy_processors_intro: We don't sell or share personal information for marketing. A small set of infrastructure providers process it on our behalf:
privacy_processors_cloudflare_body: Hosts and serves the site, provides security features (including the Turnstile bot check), and briefly processes request data like IP addresses in operational logs.
privacy_processors_turso_body: The database where form submissions, waitlist entries, accounts, and security logs are stored.
privacy_processors_resend_body: Delivers our transactional email — contact acknowledgements, waitlist notifications, verification and password-reset messages.
privacy_processors_sanity_body: Manages the site's published content (news, research, team pages). It never receives anything you submit through a form.
privacy_retention_body: Contact messages and waitlist entries are kept while they're relevant — until we've handled the conversation or the early-access program they belong to has run its course. Account data is kept while your account exists. Security logs have no automatic expiry today; we keep them for investigating abuse. You can ask us to delete any of it — including log entries about you — at any time.
privacy_rights_body: You can ask what we hold about you, ask us to correct it, or ask us to delete it. Email us from the address in question and we'll act on it promptly. If you have an account, you can also update your details or change your password yourself from your account page.
privacy_security_body: The site is served only over HTTPS, passwords are stored as salted hashes, access to stored data is limited to the people who need it to run the site, and admin surfaces sit behind authentication and rate limiting. No system is perfectly secure, but we keep the amount of data we hold deliberately small.
privacy_children_body: This site is aimed at professionals and isn't directed at children under 13. We don't knowingly collect their information; if you believe a child has submitted personal data, contact us and we'll delete it.
privacy_changes_body: If we change how we handle personal information, we'll update this page and its date. Significant changes will be called out on the page itself.
privacy_contact_body: For privacy questions or data requests, reach us at:
